dame.is · design audit · 27 October 2026 · day 12,227

Finishing the book

dame.is has something most personal sites lack: a point of view you can recognise at a glance. The ruled “dame is…” sentence, one serif voice, square hairline geometry, a palette that follows Dame’s own sky, and an x-ray that shows the record behind the page add up to something no template produces. What follows is not a case against that idea. It marks the places where the idea hasn’t been carried all the way through, and draws what carrying it through would look like.

  • 130verified findings
  • 12high
  • 59medium
  • 59low
  • 13mockups

Three things matter most

  • The sky has no contrast floor. The quiet ink that carries every timestamp, every ledger verb and the hero’s “dame is” passes AA in only 2 of 24 hours: 2.49:1 at 6 am, 2.63:1 at 7 pm. See c-02.
  • The ledger keeps its desktop grid on a phone. At 390px Dame’s words get a 206px column, about 27 characters a line, and the labels shrink to 9.6px. See c-01.
  • Some paths break. On ten record types the section crumb leads to a 404; Back can leave the site from a deep link; on a small phone the compass — the only way into the menu — is pushed off-screen. See c-07 and c-05.

Behind those are quieter gaps. The book devices the brief depends on (drop caps, a reading measure, end-marks, colophons) are designed but never reach the essays. The collections open as text lists, with their pictures behind a toggle most visitors will never find. The mid-level components have been rebuilt page by page. Almost every fix reuses something the codebase already has.

What’s working, and must be protected

  • The hero sentence is a true signature. “dame is” + role + clause on hairline rules that continue under every wrapped line — handwriting on ledger paper, at every hour and both widths.
  • One serif voice, applied strictly. All visible text is Crimson Pro; IBM Plex Mono appears only for at:// URIs, CIDs and code.
  • The sky is an idea nobody else has. At 6 am navy-and-amber, 7 pm indigo-and-orchid and 9 pm plum-black, the pages have a mood no stock theme has.
  • Disciplined geometry. Every radius is 0, rules are 1px hairlines, icons are drawn at the hairline’s weight, and there are no stray shadows.
  • Running heads that teach the protocol. The breadcrumb strip prints the day and the lexicon under you — a book’s running head, adapted to AT Protocol.
  • X-ray on an essay. Sidenotes in the margin and an “Atmosphere record” tree opposite: the best book-meets-protocol moment on the site.
  • Strong detail pages. The moth-night gallery, the Ratioed piece, the album pages and the PUBLISHED / ELAPSED colophon are the templates the rest should learn from.
  • Sound engineering underneath. No horizontal overflow in any capture, one shared column for chrome and content, principled motion, a visible focus ring, 44px touch hit areas.

What not to change: square corners, the single serif, hairline rules, the single always-on sky theme (no warm-paper blend, no silent OS dark-mode swap), the ledger as the home feed’s form, and Dame’s tuned chrome colours. Every proposal here works inside these.

The mockups

Each concept shows the current screen, then the proposal drawn in the site’s own type and palette — the real sky tokens at the hour named — with numbered notes, the tradeoff, and pointers into the code. Third-party images are drawn as placeholders; the moth photographs and sky avatars are Dame’s own.

The ledger

On a phone, verb and time ride above the post; on a desk, the time moves in beside it

At 390px the ledger keeps its three desktop columns, so Dame's posts get 206px (about 27 characters a line) and the labels shrink to 9.6px; on desktop the time sits 212–480px from what it dates, and nothing says a row is a link. Proposed: a one-line running head over full-width content on phones, a 34em measure with the time beside it on desktop, and two real links per row — the gerund to its section, the time to the record.

Desktop, 1200px at 1 pm. The same thread as the desktop crop above, in a 1200×800 viewport. The pointer is on the 1:27 am row's “posting”; the 1:46 am continuation's time has keyboard focus. Chrome labels are drawn in --ink-muted so the frame passes AA; the live strip uses --ink-faint.

  1. 1A running head. Below about 36rem each row opens with one line: the gerund at left (14px italic, the italic gerund of the section titles) and the time at right (13px, tabular). It replaces the 80px and 56px label columns, so the record gets the whole 358px. LAY-01, FEED-01, MOB-02
  2. 2Full-width body. Dame's text at 17px/1.4 runs 46–54 characters a line instead of about 27; the image and the quote box run edge to edge at 358px instead of 206px. FEED-01, MOB-02, TYP-11
  3. 3One baseline for the day. “Today” at 18px, its tally in 13px small caps on the same baseline — up from 9.6px. MOB-02
  4. 4Continuations keep their time. A thread follow-on shows only its time, right-aligned under the dashed rule — and that time is now a link, so the 20–25 continuation rows among home's first 71 can be reached by keyboard. FEED-01, FEED-03
  5. 5Labels that hold at every hour. At 7 pm --accent is 4.05:1 and --ink-muted 3.98:1 on the page; mixed 25% and 20% toward --ink they reach 4.73:1 and 4.57:1, their worst hour. Today's --ink-faint labels run 2.49–4.02:1. MOB-02
  6. 6A status reads as a sentence. The label becomes “logging” (a link to /logging) instead of “dame.is”, and the status keeps its subject: “dame is playing tennis”, in the hero's own words. LAY-01, NAV-04
  7. 7A night of moths. With the width back, the specimen strip grows from 36px to 56px thumbnails. “mothing” goes to /mothing; “10:39 pm” goes to the night's own page, /mothing/2026-10-16. NAV-04, FEED-03
  8. 8One edge, time beside it. Text, link cards and repost boxes all stop at one 34em edge, and the time column follows 12px later, so a time sits about 40px past its content instead of 212–480px. Row rules stop at the time and leave a clean right margin. The measure itself stays near today's (about 89 characters) — posts run one to three lines. FEED-07, LAY-04
  9. 9A row says it's a link. On hover (pointer devices only) a 2px accent bar appears in the left gutter and the gerund and time underline. No wash, no shadow; touch keeps today's whole-row tap. INT-07, FEED-03
  10. 10Visible focus. Tab stops on every row's time, continuations included, with a square 2px accent ring offset 2px — at least 4.05:1 against the page at all five hours (3:1 needed). FEED-03
  11. 11Two links, two jobs. The gerund, now in the italic of the section titles, goes to its section — the browser's status line reads dame.is/posting; “reposting” goes to /?verbs=reposting. The time is the record's permalink, like a page number. NAV-04
The tradeoff. The running head costs one 20px line per row and full-width photos are taller, so image-heavy days scroll further on a phone even as text rows get shorter (the feed lens's CSS prototype came out about level overall). On desktop the ledger stops at 744px, so hero, chrome and ledger no longer share a right edge, and home's time column parts company with the far-right “page numbers” of /blogging and /creating unless those flat ledgers take the same width. Moving the record link from the gerund to the time changes what a returning reader's click on “posting” does. And a static color-mix floor makes the labels darker by day (6.9–7.6:1 at 1 pm, against 3.8:1 now); deriving the label inks per hour in skyTheme.js would keep them quieter.

The sky palette

A sky that stays legible at every hour, and paper by day

The hour's faint ink (the ‘dame is’ lead, every ledger verb and time, the day's stats) clears 4.5:1 only at 7 am and 9 am, and by day the chrome's cyan spills onto photo mats. Proposed: after each hour is derived, solve its text inks against its own page, keep in-page surfaces one quiet step off that page, and paint the right sky from the very first frame.

A cold load at 1 pm, proposed. The first frame is already the tuned 1 pm sky, with the hero in place and a skeleton shaped like the ledger. Snapshot rows replace the bars where they stand. The two live posts newer than the snapshot (3:22 pm and 3:17 pm) wait behind a running-head note instead of pushing the rows down.

  1. 1Solve the inks after the sky is derived. Step each text token's lightness away from its ground, keeping hue and saturation, until it clears 4.5:1. Faint and accent are solved on --page and the raised pair on both chrome surfaces. Quote and link cards sit one nest step off the page, where a page floor drops to about 4.13, so they get their own solved pair, as the chrome already does (7 pm: faint #c7b2ca, accent #e1a5d8). Muted is then lifted to at least 1.15× faint's ratio so the ramp can't invert; at 7 pm a plain floor would leave faint at 4.58, above muted at 4.53. MOB-01's 7 pm #bfa7c3 computes to 4.499, so the solver lands on #c0a9c4. Midnight (4.02 today) is floored too. MOB-01, IDN-02, FEED-04.
  2. 2‘dame is’ stays a lead, not a smudge. At 6 am it goes from 2.49 to 4.57:1. It is still the quietest of the three tones, a grey-rose under the near-white role and the amber clause, so the sentence keeps its grammar at the hour it is most often screenshotted. IDN-02.
  3. 3Chrome labels clear AA on both bar surfaces. ‘Listening to’, ‘followed by’ and ‘on day’ use --sky-ink-faint-raised. That is solved against both --surface-raised and --surface-deep: 4.07 → 4.52 at 6 am, 3.78 → 4.53 at 7 pm. The sub-rows also step up to the 13 px metadata size, so their small caps land at 12.35 px rather than 11.4. MOB-01, TYP-01.
  4. 4The ledger's columns become readable columns. The day stats and the verb and time labels move from 2.49:1 to 4.57:1, and from 11.2 px to one 13 px metadata size. They are still clearly marginalia: smaller and quieter than the post text, and set on the same faint hue. FEED-04, TYP-01.
  5. 5Nothing under 12 px on phones. The ×0.8 step that set verb, time and day stats at 9.6 px is gone. They use the same 13 px metadata token as desktop, in the floored lilac. ‘posting’ and ‘3:17 pm’ still fit today's 5rem and 3.5rem columns. TYP-01, MOB-01.
  6. 6The accent fill mixes toward the hour's ink, not black. At night, mixing toward #000 darkens the fill toward its dark label. Mixing 15% toward --ink (the same trick --danger already uses) gives the 7 pm Resume label 3.31 → 4.89:1. By day nothing visibly moves (1 pm: 6.02 → 6.11). The accent floor takes 7 pm links from 4.05 to 4.52. IDN-02, MOB-01.
  7. 7Paper by day: photos on the page itself. --page-edge stops scaling with surfaceSep, so the tuned 1 pm chrome keeps its cyan but the tiles lose the #b7f1fa mat. A 1 px ink-12% keyline holds each photo's edge, and the caption sits on the page. “Paper” here means the hour's own page, not a warm neutral. IDN-01.
  8. 8A ribbon you can actually hit. The 24 swatches of 10×20 px become one 44 px press-and-drag slider (role="slider", aria-valuetext) with hairline hour divisions. It gets a --rule outline so no hour loses its edge, ticks at 12a · 6a · 12p · 6p, an ink thumb with its hour tag, and 44×44 steppers. The open chip's label moves to --ink: today it is accent on an accent tint, 3.88:1 at 1 pm. MOB-07.
  9. 9Held is not live. When the sky is held, the header says ‘Held at 7 pm’ and offers an outlined ‘Return to live’ button. The accent caret stays on the real hour, and the bar's hour chip turns dashed, so the state survives closing the sheet. Live gets a small accent square and the current hour. INT-06.
  10. 10The right sky from frame one. A 24-hour palette table inlined in <head>, with the tuning baked in at build, means the first paint is the tuned hour, with no parchment and no untuned cyan. The ledger-shaped skeleton holds the feed's place. Live records merge by key, and newer ones wait behind ‘2 new entries’. INT-02, IDN-13.
The tradeoff. The floors flatten dawn and dusk. At 6 am and 7 pm there is only 9.4:1 and 7.5:1 of room between page and ink, so at 7 pm faint, muted and soft land at 4.58, 5.33 and 5.57:1. Their difference has to come from size, small caps and italic rather than lightness, and the 7 pm ‘dame is’ is a little less moody than the dusky mauve the owner tuned. The solver also outranks inkWarmth/inkContrast whenever they would go below the floor, so the Sky studio must show the solved value, or the owner will tune a colour that never ships. The ribbon shows the avatar's sky, not the page you'll get: noon is cyan in the strip but near-white on screen. Dropping the mats removes the tiles' card-like “this opens” cue, so the keyline, hover lift and zoom-in cursor must carry it. A 13 px metadata size no longer fits ‘photographing’ in the 5rem mobile verb column; that needs the stacked running head proposed elsewhere, or a 5.5rem column. Finally, the inlined palette table duplicates about 1 KB of data that prefetch.mjs must regenerate. A tuning change published between deploys still lands on the second paint, as it does today.

Build notes

  • src/lib/skyTheme.js: add a solveContrast(vars, day) pass at the end of paletteForHour (:431), after applyOverride (:382–408). It nudges HSL L by 0.005 away from the page for --sky-ink-faint (≥4.5 vs --sky-page), --sky-ink-muted (≥max(4.5, 1.15×faint)), --sky-accent (≥4.5), and --sky-ink-faint-raised/-muted-raised (≥4.5 vs both --sky-surface-raised and --sky-surface-deep). The unfloored offsets live at :235 and :289.
  • Test: loop h0–23 with the is.dame.sky snapshot next to src/lib/skyTuning.test.js and assert every ratio above, so a future tuning record can't regress it. Surface the per-hour ratio row in SkyThemeStudio.jsx.
  • Cards: PostEmbed.css paints quote and link cards one nest step off the page (:73–74, :144–145). Re-scope --ink-faint/--ink-muted/--accent there to values solved against that surface, exactly as theme.css:275–279 does for .chrome-bar with the -raised pair.
  • src/styles/app.css:249–269 .home-hero-cta-primary: change color-mix(… var(--accent) 90%, #000) to 85%, var(--ink) (border 72%, hover 78%). Make the same change to .chrome-nav-bottom:hover at ChromeBar.css:669.

Photographs: Era 1 (Part II)

createdJanuary 1, 2011
elapsed16 years ago
taggedart

Selected images from early in my photographic journey.

11
1 pm

/creating/photographs-era-1-part-i at 1 pm, desktop (75%). Title, colophon and text stay on the 588px measure (between the dashed guides); the series runs in justified rows across the 980px frame the stylesheet already computes. The photographs are the series’ own, in order, at their real 3:2 and 2:3 ratios.

  1. 1A view switch on the page, for this page. ‘plates · index’ in small caps beside the intro replaces two glyphs with no visible label that appear only while the compass menu is open. /creating and /curating open on plates; a visitor’s choice is kept per section, and the home feed keeps its own ledger preference. COL-01, IDN-04
  2. 2Kind and year, not age. One small-caps line, ‘software · 2026’. The year is what a portfolio needs; ‘1mo ago’ goes stale, and today all seven works from 2025 read ‘1y ago’ while the 2011 photographs read ‘15y ago’ here and ‘16 years ago’ on their own page. COL-08
  3. 3A title page for works without a cover. A rule inset 12px, kind top-left, title centred, year bottom-right, on the paper. It replaces the blank 4:3 box with a lone ❧. Three records have no cover or image: CodeTV Appearance, Ratioed, and ‘An Early Collaboration with an LLM…’. COL-11
  4. 4Covers as plates. Every cover is cropped to 4:3 and set on bare paper with a neutral 1px keyline (ink at 14%). No cyan mat, no card, no lift on hover: hover darkens the keyline. A grid in reading order, row by row, replaces the round-robin masonry, so newest-first reads left to right. IDN-06, COL-01
  5. 5Two-up plates on phones. 173px covers with the same caption beneath: the 21 works take 11 rows, and every one shows its picture. The fixed 4:3 crop keeps each row’s covers level, however long the titles run. COL-01
  6. 6The year as the index’s folio. ‘index’ is today’s ledger with the age column replaced by the year. The year appears once per run, with a dotted leader down to the run’s last work, so the column reads 2026 to 2011 like a book’s index. Screen readers still hear every year. COL-08
  7. 7Each channel shows what it holds. The title, the are.na description in italic where the channel has one, then the first six blocks in curated order, cropped square. Text blocks stay as text, so ‘words i’d never heard of until now’ shows its words. IDN-04, COL-01
  8. 8Count and date as a folio. ‘158 blocks’ at the right edge, with ‘updated October 26, 2026’ beneath. Curating.jsx already loads the description and updatedAt, and the ledger throws both away. The word stays ‘blocks’, because channels mix images, text and links. COL-01, COL-08
  9. 9A three-up contact sheet on phones. 117px squares with 4px gutters and a hairline round each, cropped to fill, on the paper rather than a cyan mat: fifteen or more images a screen instead of one. 222 blocks make 74 rows, about 9,300px instead of 82,547px. The lightbox still shows each image whole. COL-02, LAY-03, IDN-06
  10. 10The lightbox as a tipped-in plate. A 1px neutral keyline replaces the 40px soft shadow, and a caption says where the image came from. Block 3’s are.na title is a filename (‘0_0-1-.jpeg’), so the channel stands in, followed by ‘are.na · connected November 2, 2024 · record ↗’. Swiping steps through the images, as the arrow keys do; the counter stops being aria-hidden. INT-14
  11. 11Photo series run wider than the text. Galleries use --doc-overhang, which already reaches the 980px frame but is used only by Ratioed. Justified rows (each photo’s flex-grow set by its aspect ratio) end flush, so a portrait beside a landscape no longer leaves a hole: three landscapes, then two landscapes and a portrait. COL-04, LAY-09
  12. 12Numbered plates. ‘pl. 1’ to ‘pl. 17’ in small caps under each photograph. All 17 image blocks in this record have empty alt text, so for now the plate number is the only label each image has. The URL says part-i and the title says Part II; one of them is wrong in the record. IDN-06, COL-04
The tradeoff. Plates are heavier. /creating’s default view would load 21 covers, and /curating’s about 114 thumbnails (19 channels × 6), where the ledger loads none. The page already waits on the first covers before revealing (COVER_WAIT), so small srcset thumbnails, lazy loading below the fold and an index default under Save-Data matter more. The curating snapshot also has to carry six thumbnails per channel, not just one cover. Per-section memory adds a second way to see the same list and one more stored key per section. The global ledger default was a deliberate choice, so it stays for the home feed, and this proposal changes only the collections. Cropping to 4:3 and to squares trims the edges of some images; the work page and the lightbox still show them whole. The typographic plate only works if it stays the exception: three of 21 works today. If most works lacked covers, the sheet would become a wall of ruled boxes.

Build notes

  • Per-section view: add a useSectionView(section, fallback) hook next to src/hooks/useFeedLayout.jsx, keyed dame.view.creating / dame.view.curating. Like the existing hook, it stores only an explicit choice. Creating.jsx:101-102 and Curating.jsx:85-86 read it instead of the global layout. The switch is a two-button role="group" with aria-pressed, rendered beside PageShell’s intro (add a slot after .page-intro). LayoutToggle (rendered at ChromeBar.jsx:682) keeps its ‘Home feed layout’ label and stops re-skinning the sections.
  • Plates: replace MasonryGrid on these two pages with a CSS grid, repeat(auto-fill, minmax(min(16rem, 46%), 1fr)), which gives 3-up at 1008px and 2-up at 358px. .creating-grid-link img gets aspect-ratio: 4/3; object-fit: cover. Drop the --page-edge background, border-radius and translateY(-2px) in src/pages/Creating.css, and use outline: 1px solid color-mix(in srgb, var(--ink) 14%, transparent) for the keyline.
  • Typographic plate: rewrite .creating-grid-placeholder (Creating.jsx:36-39, Creating.css:54-62) to render workCategory(v), v.title and the year from v.createdAt inside an inset rule, instead of the ❧.
  • Dates: the index folio and plate captions use new Date(v.createdAt).getFullYear(); retire relativeTime at Creating.jsx:43 (cards) and :168 (ledger). COL-08 asks for old-style figures, but the Crimson Pro the site loads from Google Fonts has none: its GSUB lists only ccmp dnom frac liga locl numr pnum tnum (checked with fontTools; small caps are synthesized too). The mockup therefore sets years in lining figures. onum would need a self-hosted cut that has it, which is worth checking upstream before promising. FlatLedger gets an optional runStart flag per row to draw the dotted leader. Curating dates use formatDateFull (src/lib/time.js:155).
  • Curating rows: in scripts/prefetch.mjs (the gallery object at about line 823), add strip: snap.blocks.slice(0, 6).map(normalizeBlock) next to cover. Render text blocks with the existing .curating-text-card idiom, minus its --surface-raised fill.
  • Phone grid: below 34rem, src/pages/Curating.css:12 becomes repeat(3, minmax(0, 1fr)) with gap: 4px; wider screens keep the 11rem track. (COL-02’s minmax(min(7rem, 30%), 1fr)) also works on phones, but on desktop it would give eight columns.) .curating-block-button loses padding, the --page-edge fill and the hover lift, and its img goes from object-fit: contain to cover.
  • Lightbox: in src/components/Lightbox.css:69, replace box-shadow with outline: 1px solid color-mix(in srgb, var(--ink) 22%, transparent). Add a caption row to the controls in Lightbox.jsx (around the counter at line 285, which loses aria-hidden). Use pointer-drag stepping that is off under reduced motion.
  • Galleries: add { value: 'justified' } to GALLERY_LAYOUTS in src/components/LeafletDocument.jsx (each figure flex: var(--ar) 1 0 from the block’s aspectRatio), and give .leaflet-gallery margin-inline: calc(-1 * var(--doc-overhang)) (Blogging.css:130; RatioedBlock.css:29 is the precedent). Plate numbers come from ::before on a CSS counter.
  • Contrast as drawn: the small-caps lines use --ink-muted at 1 pm (6.19:1 on --page) and 9 pm (5.89:1). At 7 pm --ink-muted is 3.98:1, so the mockup uses color-mix(in srgb, var(--ink-muted) 50%, var(--ink)) = 5.55:1. Today’s --ink-faint (3.79:1 at 1 pm) would fail for these captions; that fix belongs to the palette concept.

9pm

Phones at 9 pm (sky-21). Left: the whole /mothing index, about 1,400px as drawn against 33,006px today. Each night is a folio line, a four-cell strip, its counts and a link you can see without hovering. Right: the night page scrolled to its first lifer, with six moths on one screen where today there is one.

  1. 1One figures component, everywhere a page counts. Hairline-ruled cells, the numeral first so every numeral sits on one baseline, a small-caps label beneath and an optional one-line note. It is the Ratioed table in the /mothing voice: ink numerals at weight 400, accent labels, no boxes. On a phone the short figures go three-up and the time span takes its own full-width row, so no orphaned tile is left over. “Sessions” becomes “nights” to match the page's own words. This is the component's /mothing use; c-11 proposes it for the rest of the site. LAY-06, COL-07.
  2. 2Most seen becomes six plates. Each plate is a square photo, the name in serif and the count as ×12. Nothing breaks mid-name any more (“Green / Cutworm Moth”), and a tap opens the photo in the existing lightbox, as a tile does today. Halysidota has no common name, so its genus is set in italic. COL-03.
  3. 3Nights are grouped by season, and older seasons fold. A small-caps season header carries its dates and tally (2 nights · 34 moths · 27 species). Only the current season is open, so the page goes from 32,683px to under two screens and renders 22 thumbnails where it now renders 519 rows. COL-03.
  4. 4Each night is one ruled entry. A folio on the left (No. 29, Oct 16, Friday), a filmstrip of the first eight photographs at 72px ending in a “+7” cell, then the counts, the time at the light and a first-sightings count that uses the chip's existing count form. COL-03, IDN-06.
  5. 5The way in is visible at rest. “see the night →” is accent text with a resting --accent-soft underline, and the folio and filmstrip link to the same page. Touch screens, which never hover, now get the cue. COL-03.
  6. 6The full ledger stays. The existing one-row-per-observation ledger becomes the index you choose, for searching by name, and stops being the page's default. COL-03 → COL-01.
  7. 7Plates on paper. The photo sits on the page with a neutral --ink 12% keyline, not on a --page-edge caption slab (cyan at 1 pm) and not with a 2px hover lift. Hover darkens the keyline instead. The crop stays square, because a species drawer reads best in an even grid and the lightbox shows the whole frame. IDN-06.
  8. 8A specimen label. The time in small caps, the common name in serif, the binomial in italic and the first-sighting chip on its own line when it applies. The time now appears on the night page as well as in the ledger. COL-02, LAY-03.
  9. 9Two-up on a phone. minmax(min(12rem, 46%), 1fr) gives 2 × 171px on a 358px column and leaves desktop at four-up. At 9 pm the scrolled view holds six moths where today it holds one. The audit's two-column prototype measured 2,785px against today's 7,255px. COL-02, LAY-03.
  10. 10The night entry on a phone. The folio collapses to one line, the strip to four cells, and the counts and link move below. The season tally drops species so that it stays on one line. COL-03.
The tradeoff. The index stops showing every moth. A visitor who searches the page for a name finds it only in the open season, unless the fold is a <details> (which Chromium's find-in-page opens) or they switch to the ledger. Most seen needs a photo for each species, picked by rule (the latest sighting of that taxon), and the rule will sometimes pick a poor frame. Fixing that means curating by hand. A 72px square can cut a wing, and the strip can show the same species twice in a row (both Spotted Beet Webworms on Oct 16), which deduplicating by taxon would avoid. Meteorological seasons are a Northern Hemisphere choice, and a lone winter night would become a season with one entry. On phones each plate shrinks from 358px to 171px, so identification detail moves behind one tap into the lightbox. Renaming “session” to “night” changes four labels in Mothing.jsx and MothingNight.jsx. The record field sessionCount keeps its name.

Build notes

  • src/pages/Mothing.jsx 189–208: replace .mothing-stats and the run-in .mothing-toplist with a shared <Figures> (model: .ratioed-piece-figures in src/pages/RatioedPiece.css 55–75, with the numeral first and the label beneath) and a Most seen plate row. stats.topSpecies (computeStats, src/lib/inaturalist.js) has taxonId but no photo, so take the newest observations entry with that taxon and use photoUrl(photo, 'small').
  • src/pages/Mothing.jsx 218–264: render one <NightEntry> per buildSessions() session in place of the per-observation ledger. Its parts are photographed(session).slice(0, 8), nightSummaryParts(), nightPath() (all in src/lib/mothing.js) and <FirstSightingChip count={n}>, where n counts firstIds.has(o.id). Strip thumbs are srcSet square 1x and small 2x, loading="lazy".

Chrome

The chrome steps aside while you read, and every tool says what it does

Mid-post today, a quarter of a laptop screen and a fifth of a phone is pinned chrome (225 of 900px, 175 of 844px), the bottom bar is a row of identical wordless squares, and at 320px the compass falls off the screen. Proposed: one running-head line while you read, with the atmosphere as a masthead that scrolls away; small-caps words beside the desktop tools and first-visit captions on phones; and a priority order that keeps the compass on screen at any width.

Now

Proposed

dame.is
/blogging /Why I started posting like it's the 2000s again
site.standard.document

Back then, social media was a place you went to keep up with what your friends were actually doing. You didn't go there to consume the news, follow influencers, or debate culture war issues with strangers.

Social media was a digital location for the expression of your state of being. After all, the word "is" is the 3rd-person singular present indicative of the word "be", which means "to exist or live" as in Shakespeare's existential question: "To be or not to be..."

But overtime, most social media websites shifted towards prompting you with questions like "What's on your mind?" (Facebook) or "What's happening?" (Twitter) instead of asking for a simple update about the state of your current existence. These subtle UI changes turned out to be massively consequential for how we experience reality in the 2020s, a time period in which social media has finally worked its way inside almost every facet of our lives.

image source: chscommunicator

While I'm glad that the concept of "posting" on social media evolved over time, I am sad that we seemed to essentially abandoned the traditional "status update" of Facebook's yesteryears in the process. I wish people still made simple reports of what they were doing, eating, reading, or listening to.

I think this loss is part of a larger phenomenon of everyone becoming much more disembodied and less grounded while we're inhabiting digital spaces. To help combat this shift in my own life, I decided to create a new personal website this year that felt more "alive" and reflective of my lived experience.

/blogging /Why I started posting like it's the 2000s again
site.standard.document

Why I started posting like it's the 2000s again

Published
January 29, 2025
Elapsed
2 years ago

In November of 2007, Facebook made a tiny change to its user interface that would massively influence what we know of today as a "post" on social media. What was that change?

They removed the mandatory word "is" from the beginning of what were once called "status updates".

Initially, the status format forced you to write about yourself in the third person; you couldn't get rid of the verb "is" after your name, so getting your feelings across often required some grammatical maneuvering. (source)

In those days, all of our posts looked like this:

Dame is watching a movie

About this site

A key to the two bars

  • atmosphereWhat Dame is doing, listening to, and the readings from Dame's phone. It sits at the top of every page.
  • skyThe palette follows the sky in Dame's hourly avatar, on Eastern time. Pick an hour to see it.
  • filterChoose which kinds of records a feed shows.
  • inspectTurn the page inside out: every block shows the AT Protocol record behind it.
  • upOne level up the trail. It never leaves the site.
  • contentsEvery page Dame is: available, welcoming, creating, blogging…

dame.is a personal website built on top of the AT Protocol (atproto). The data behind most of what you see here is stored on an independently hosted Personal Data Server (PDS).

The tradeoff. On desktop, the live atmosphere stops being in view the whole time you read. The thing that makes the site feel inhabited goes from “always” to “at the top, or on demand”, and the owner chose “expanded by default” on purpose. The status ↔ trail swap is new motion in the running head; it should cross-fade, and be instant under reduced motion. Putting the masthead in the flow also means opening it from the top moves the page, which useTierSlide avoids today by overlaying. Words in the bar are copy someone has to maintain. First-visit captions depend on localStorage, so a visitor whose storage is blocked sees them every time. The overflow logic is the one genuinely new piece of state. It also moves ⓘ off the bar on exactly the small phones whose visitors may never open the compass; the key and the captions are the hedge. And anyone who used ← as history-back will find it now goes up.

The tradeoff. The menu stops being a minimalist list. Eleven glossed rows ask more of the eye than nine words, and the glosses are copy someone has to keep true. Folios cost the most. Each one needs the newest record in its section when the menu opens. If they are fetched on open they will flicker in, and a stale folio (“2d” when it’s really 2 mo) is worse than none. They should come from data the site already holds, or a small folio summary written alongside is.dame.nav. The veil reverses a deliberate “no tint” choice (ActionDock.css:1–7), so on desktop the sheet no longer reads as part of the chrome. Three columns change tab order to column by column and need a single-column fallback below about 900px. Dropping the per-row /path loses a quiet URL lesson on every row except the current one. While the menu is open, the compass mark is replaced by ×.

Records

Every record is a page you can land on

Feed rows and shared links land on record pages that open on a raw rkey, set the record at body size under a highlighted at:// string, and, for 10 of 17 verbs, offer a section crumb that leads to “Nowhere to be found”. Proposed: one plate for every record. The crumb names the moment and always goes somewhere, the record’s own sentence is the H1, a colophon dates it, earlier and later turn the page, and the URI drops to a folio.

One plate, three pages. The detail-page skeleton, filled for the tennis status, the essay between “How I made an automated dynamic avatar” and “A guestbook and welcome message” on /blogging, and the October 16 mothing night. Every value comes from the live pages and records; the essay’s date and day number are from its publishedAt.

  1. 1The crumb names the moment, and its parent resolves. The last crumb is a short human label (date and time for statuses, posts, plays and reposts; a title cut to about 28 characters for documents) instead of 3mysojzqy3z23. The rkey stays in x-ray and the folio. The parent is looked up in the verb registry, not copied from the path. (NAV-06, NAV-01)
  2. 2The record’s sentence is the H1. “dame is playing tennis” in the hero’s grammar and ruled lines: muted lead, the status in accent. The tab title follows. The column is pinned to the 588px measure (width: 100% on .record-page), so a short status no longer shrinks it to 484px. (NAV-06, COL-05)
  3. 3One colophon line. The verb’s past tense, then weekday, date, time and day of life in small caps, replacing “yesterday at 9:36 PM on October 26, 2026 (Day 12,226)”. The relative age stays in the footer (“written 19h ago”). (COL-05, COL-06)
  4. 4One row of quiet actions. “Open in…” keeps the waypoints picker. “Inspect record” switches on x-ray for this page, like the microscope, and replaces the boxed “Inspect Data”. A play’s Apple Music and Spotify links join this row instead of stacking a second button style above it. (COL-05)
  5. 5Earlier and later turn the page. A ruled strip in the MothingNight earlier/later pattern: the previous status and how long before, the next one or “none yet”, and a centred link up to the whole section. Labels are 12px small caps in --ink-muted, 6.19:1 on --page at 1 pm. (COL-05, NAV-09, COL-06)
  6. 6The URI becomes a folio. 12px IBM Plex Mono in --ink-muted, centred, unhighlighted, breaking only after a slash (<wbr>) instead of mid-token. Copying and exploring it stay one tap away in x-ray. (COL-05)
  7. 7↖ means up, not history. The bar’s back control goes to the same resolved parent as the crumb and says so (“Up to logging”), so a visitor who arrived from a Bluesky link isn’t sent back off the site. History stays with the browser’s own Back. (NAV-11, NAV-01)
  8. 8“reposting” goes somewhere. It links to /reposting, one of the indexes generated for verbs that have no page of their own, and ↖ uses the same path. Flushing’s crumb stays plain text while vercel.json redirects /flushing to flushes.app. (NAV-01)
  9. 9A repost says whose post it is. “dame reposted Poe”: muted subject, ink verb, accent name. Poe’s post follows as a quotation in the embed treatment, dated by Poe’s own clock, and the “dame reposted 2h ago” kicker becomes the colophon. (NAV-06)
  10. 10Empty replies take one line. “Replies · none yet · reply on Bluesky” replaces the heading over 150px of blank space. It stays on reposts, where it follows the reposted post’s thread. (COL-05)
  11. 11/reposting is a real page. The home ledger, filtered through the ?verbs= state that FeedFilters already reads, under a hero in the site’s grammar, “dame is reposting”. A small-caps line says what’s filtered and clears it. Day headers, the NSID running head and x-ray work as they do on the home page. (NAV-01)
  12. 12Vitals stay with their status. When a status carries a stateRef, the live VitalsChip sits under the colophon: 62 bpm, in vehicle, 1099 cal for the possums. “playing tennis” has no stateRef, so the desktop page shows none. (COL-05)
  13. 13Not-found speaks the site’s language. “dame is nowhere to be found”, the requested path in mono, the likeliest page (the home page’s Projects button already goes to /creating), then the menu’s list. The footer drops “written — · updated —”. (NAV-14)
  14. 14One plate for every detail page. Running head, title, colophon, body, actions, replies, foot, folio. Records, essays, works, albums, nights and Ratioed takes fill the same slots, and the in-page “← Albums / ← Mothing / ← Ratioed” links go: the pinned crumb is the one way up. (COL-06, SYS-10, NAV-11)
  15. 15Essays end with a next page. After the comments: the previous and next essays by date and “all 7 essays”. Works on /creating get the same foot. (NAV-09)
The tradeoff. Earlier and later cost a lookup on every record page. The feed snapshot keeps only the newest 50–500 records of each collection (reposts: 200, none older than 90 days), so older records need a listRecords call either side of the rkey, and the strip has to wait for it or fill in late. The same limit means /reposting lists only what the snapshot holds unless it pages live. Setting times by Dame’s clock means a visitor in London reads 5:36 pm for what was 9:36 pm for them; the footer’s relative “19h ago” still tells them how long ago it was. Nine generated indexes add routes that need OG cards and prerendering, and some, like /liking, may not deserve a page; the plain-text crumb is the fallback for those. And a long status set as the H1 still takes three ruled lines on a phone.

Set essays like a book: one text block, a drop cap, a 66-character line, and the next essay at the end

Today a blog post opens flat (the drop-cap rule never matches LeafletDocument’s markup), runs about 85 characters a line, signals paragraphs two ways, prints straight quotes in a 48px title and stops at the reply thread. The proposal sets the same record as a book page. The text hangs from the chrome’s edge, the facts move into the margin, and the essay ends with ❧ and the next essay.

Why I started posting like it’s the 2000s again

Published
January 29, 2025
Elapsed
2 years ago
Essay
1 of 7 in blogging
Edition
bafyreihf…tda inspect

In November of 2007, Facebook made a tiny change to its user interface that would massively influence what we know of today as a “post” on social media. What was that change?

They removed the mandatory word “is” from the beginning of what were once called “status updates”.

Initially, the status format forced you to write about yourself in the third person; you couldn’t get rid of the verb “is” after your name, so getting your feelings across often required some grammatical maneuvering. (source)Sourcethe-independent.com

In those days, all of our posts looked like this:

Dame is watching a movie

Dame is hanging out with friends

Dame is sad

Back then, social media was a place you went to keep up with what your friends were actually doing. You didn’t go there to consume the news, follow influencers, or debate culture war issues with strangers.

Social media was a digital location for the expression of your state of being. After all, the word “is” is the 3rd-person singular present indicative of the word “be”, which means “to exist or live” as in Shakespeare’s existential question: “To be or not to be…”

For speed and efficiency’s sake, I created an Apple Shortcut that is triggered via my iPhone’s Action Button that allows me to quickly type in the update and have it sent to the Bluesky account via the API. This allows me to post an update in less than 15 seconds from either my phone or my watch.

Here’s a template of the shortcut I use if you’re interested in seeing it in action: shortcut link

What other helpful frameworks from the web’s past have we accidentally discarded? What new methods might we create to foster more groundedness in our digital lives?

The end of the essay, 9 pm: desktop at 65%, and a phone. A ❧ closes the text, then an earlier/later block in the same voice as mothing’s “Earlier night / Later night”. This is the first essay, so the earlier cell says so instead of disappearing. The replies follow, unchanged apart from a lifted tone for their small text. On the phone the later essay comes first. Avatars are placeholders.

  1. 1A typeset title (TYP-07, TYP-13). it’s takes a real apostrophe at 48px, and text-wrap: balance breaks the title into two even lines. This is a display-only pass, so the record keeps its straight tick (see 11).
  2. 2One left edge (LAY-05). The breadcrumb, title and text block all start at the chrome’s edge: x = 96 at 1200px, 230 at 1440. Today the column is centred and starts 196px right of the breadcrumb. The freed right side becomes the margin.
  3. 3Facts in the margin (LAY-05, NAV-09). The Published / Elapsed band becomes a colophon beside the title, with two new rows. “Essay 1 of 7” is a page number for the blog. “Edition” is the record’s CID, which x-ray already calls “this exact version”. Under about 62rem it folds back into the band (10).
  4. 4The drop cap returns (IDN-03, TYP-02). The rule already exists but never matched .leaflet-doc > p.leaflet-paragraph. Here it is a three-line accent ‘I’ via initial-letter: 3 (Firefox keeps its tuned float). The rest of the first line is in letterspaced small caps.
  5. 5A 66-character line (TYP-03, TYP-13). The body is 20/31 in a 28em (560px) measure. Measured on this essay’s paragraphs in Crimson Pro, that gives a median of 66 characters a line (60–72), against 85 (75–93) at today’s 16.8px in 588px. The brief suggested 34em at 19px, but that measures a median of 84, so 28em at 20px is used instead. The measure is set in em of the body, not ch of the zero. Paragraphs get text-wrap: pretty, but in Chromium it does not engage next to an initial letter, so on the phone the first paragraph still ends on “change?” by itself.
  6. 6One paragraph signal (TYP-04). Paragraphs are separated by an indent only, with no extra 16px gap after the first paragraph of a run. Vertical space appears only around insets, figures and headings. The paragraph after one of those breaks starts flush, so a break is never marked twice.
  7. 7A real quotation, sourced in the margin (TYP-04, LAY-05). The italic source passage is inset on the existing 2px accent-soft blockquote rule, and its text lines up with the paragraph indent. The author sets the inset; it is not guessed from italics. Its link also gets a sidenote naming the host.
  8. 8Examples as a stack (TYP-04). The three “Dame is …” lines are inset, unindented and 4px apart, so they read as specimens rather than three stray one-line paragraphs.
  9. 9The credit sits under its caption (TYP-04). The record’s credit block starts with “\n”, which renders a blank line and leaves the credit 75px below the caption. Trimming that newline puts it directly under the italic caption at caption size.
  10. 10Phone (TYP-02, TYP-03). The same opening at 18/28, about 47 characters a line. The margin folds into today’s band, now with a third column, “Essay 1 of 7”. The band’s labels move from --ink-faint (2.63:1 at 7 pm) to a mixed label tone that measures at least 4.88:1 at all five sample hours.
  11. 11X-ray shows the manuscript (TYP-07). With inspect on, each block’s tag sits in the same margin, which fits c-12’s “x-ray as marginalia”. Paragraph 2’s note quotes the record’s own text with its four straight quotes marked. The page is the typeset copy, and the record is never rewritten.
  12. 12A heading ladder (TYP-08). H2 28px/600 with a hairline above, H3 22px italic, H4 20px/600 in the accent, H5 20px italic. Each step has about twice as much space above it as below. The 46 H4/H5 headings in the Bluesky guide stop reading as bold sentences.
  13. 13An end-mark (IDN-03, IDN-12). ❧ in the accent, centred on the text block with 3rem above and below. It is the fleuron already used as a placeholder on /creating, made the site’s one ornament.
  14. 14Earlier, later, and the whole blog (NAV-09). Essays are ordered by publishedAt. The later essay is the dynamic-avatar post (February 5, 2025), and the earlier cell says plainly that there is none. “All 7 essays in blogging” closes the block. The brief said 8, but the index and the PDS both list 7.
The tradeoff. Essays get longer, and the layout gets a second column to maintain. Measured in Crimson Pro, this essay’s 21 text blocks go from 1,747px to 2,387px tall on desktop (×1.37) and grow ×1.11 on a phone. The reply thread and the next-essay link move further down. c-05’s slimmer reading chrome wins some of that back. Hanging the column left and adding a margin touches every long-form template (posts, works, Ratioed, records, the résumé). It also breaks the figure-overhang maths in Blogging.css, which assumes a centred column, so figures can only grow to the right. The quote pass is display-only, but it has to run after facet slicing and skip links, code and handles, or it will corrupt byte offsets. It can still curl something wrongly (’90s, nested quotes), and only the x-ray note shows the original. Insets, stacks and credits depend on an author hint, so the existing 26 documents keep today’s look until someone edits them. The small caps are synthesised (the web subset has no smcp), so they look lighter than true small caps would.

Proposed: a fixed standfirst under the hero, with hold and shuffle beside the sentence; a /themself that still works without its profile record; and a 404 that gives the visitor the table of contents.

The 404, desktop and phone at 1 pm, whole page. Desktop: a mistyped address. Phone: /sharing, which renders the same page for visitors until a sharing record exists (so does /ethos, which redirects there).

  1. 1Hold and shuffle sit with the sentence. They are set in small caps on the right, under its last rule, like a folio. Shuffle moves out of the “Primary destinations” nav it was misfiled in. The rotation also stops by itself after three swaps, and whenever the hero scrolls out of view. MOB-10, INT-12.
  2. 2A standfirst that doesn’t move. Two sentences name Dame’s work and say what this page is, then “What am I looking at?” opens the ⓘ sheet. The CTA row right under it is the “start here”, so the standfirst doesn’t repeat Projects and Blog as inline links. It uses the existing .page-intro voice (18 px, --ink-soft, 10.53:1 at 1 pm), and its first words are in small caps, echoing the hero’s “dame is”. Every fact in it is already published on the site: the résumé title, the hero’s roles and clauses, and the ⓘ sheet. NAV-02.
  3. 3The CTA row is destinations only, and every one is labelled. The guestbook glyph becomes “Sign the guestbook”, its existing aria-label made visible. On a phone it wraps to a second row. Resume keeps its filled accent (--page on the fill, 6.02:1). NAV-02.
  4. 4Held. Tapping the sentence or “hold” freezes it, and a second tap resumes. The closing rule turns 2 px --accent (5.10:1 against --page at 1 pm), and the folio reads “held · resume”. That is a pause any touch user can find, which is what WCAG 2.2.2 asks for. The h1 never becomes a live region. MOB-10, INT-12.
  5. 5The card stays, and the handle becomes a link to the Bluesky profile. Nothing here waits for is.dame.profile/self, so the page no longer ends at the bio. NAV-07, COL-11.
  6. 6Find Dame is a two-column ledger of real routes in: Bluesky (6,679 followers), the one address the site publishes (resume@dame.is), the résumé and the guestbook (36 signatures). NAV-07.
  7. 7Dame is also… lists six gerund links. Each gloss is cut from that page’s own intro or stats line, and each folio is its latest record. Curating has no dated record behind it, so its folio is empty rather than a dash. NAV-07, COL-11.
  8. 8No placeholder dates. With no record behind the page, the footer prints only “Published on the AT Protocol”. Both desktop pages here fit the window, so the ↓ chip is gone as well. INT-09.
  9. 9“This page intentionally left blank.” The book idiom is set between hairlines, and the intro repeats the address that was asked for. The stray “Try the home page.” and its 1.5em indent are gone. INT-09.
  10. 10The dead end becomes a contents page. These are the compass menu’s own rows, in the same is.dame.nav order, so a wrong turn lands on the whole site. If c-06’s glossed contents ships, this list picks it up, and c-07’s “you may want…” line sits above it for near-miss paths such as /projects. Paths are set in --ink-muted on --page (6.19:1). In the menu the same paths are --ink-faint on --surface-deep, which measures 3.47:1. INT-09, NAV-02.
  11. 11/sharing stops talking to its author. With no is.dame.page/sharing record, visitors get this page and not “write one and refresh”. The hint is shown only to the signed-in owner. NAV-10, COL-11.
The tradeoff. The standfirst is the first fixed copy on a page that is otherwise all rotation and live data. It costs about 210 px on a phone (the folio row, four lines of standfirst and a second CTA row), so Today’s first post starts in the bottom fifth of the first screen instead of halfway down. It is also one more thing to keep true: if Dame’s work changes, the sentence is wrong until someone edits it, so it belongs in a record (is.dame.page/home), not in JSX. A hero that rests after three swaps means fewer visitors see the long tail of the 22 phrases (10 roles, 12 clauses), and shuffle becomes the only way to see more. The /themself fallback repeats parts of the menu and /available. Once a profile record exists, its body sits above these lists, so they should stay this compact. Turning /sharing into a 404 hides a page Dame may mean to fill.

The text is clamped to two lines with “+ more”, which expands it in place the way a listening session opens, and the link card shrinks to a reference line. The row is 111px; it was 231px. FEED-05 · IDN-05
  5. 5One clock per row. The original post’s date is a muted absolute “· Oct 26”, not an accent-coloured “1d ago” that is louder than the row’s own time. The time column stays the only clock, and the external link moves to the author’s name. FEED-11
  6. 6Media in a citation is one 60px thumbnail. The tweet screenshot that took about 190px of the seed paste soy goblin row becomes a 3.75rem thumb beside the quote. This row is 84px; it was 297px. FEED-05
  7. 7A thread is one entry. The first gutter cell says “posting” and then “thread · 3”. A 1px --accent bracket joins the members, with a tick at each one, and dashed rules between them as today. FEED-06
  8. 8The time column runs one way. A thread’s folio is its newest time (1:46 am, where the feed already anchors it) with “from 1:27” beneath. The column now reads 1:46, 1:44, 1:41, 1:37 instead of 1:27, 1:29, 1:46, 1:44. FEED-06
  9. 9Each post keeps its own time as a small margin note by its tick, like a verse number. Each one links to its post, so no member loses its permalink. FEED-06
  10. 10A quote inside a quote indents again and turns italic, with its own author line. Box-in-box nesting goes. IDN-05
  11. 11A thread that crosses midnight says so. Members from another day than the header carry the date (“Oct 26 · 8:59 pm”), and the folio reads “from Oct 26, 8:57 pm”. The thread stays whole under Today. FEED-06
  12. 12The honest horizon. The ledger stops at the oldest moment every collection still covers: the newest of each capped collection’s oldest loaded record, rounded to a whole day. A fleuron between hairlines marks the end, and one sentence says how far back it is complete. Older days are no longer labelled as if they were whole. FEED-02
  13. 13Ways on, on purpose. “Earlier:” links each gerund page, whose own history goes back further. “Load the week before” is a quiet .s-btn that fetches the next page of each collection by cursor and moves the horizon back seven days. FEED-02
  14. 14The bottom bar says where you are. The day in view, “Oct 25”, sits beside ↑ instead of a bare “546”. It is the same label the strip already reads from the day headers. FEED-02
  15. 15Running dates replace day headings on /logging. The first status of each day carries the date and day-of-life in the left margin, and a full-strength --rule starts each day. There is no 18px heading or 48px gap: a one-status day is 59px instead of about 126px. LAY-08
  16. 16“dame.is” runs into the sentence. The small-caps name reads as one line with the status: “dame.is playing tennis”. It no longer repeats in a 104px column. The time stays the row’s link (FEED-03’s permalink, drawn in c-01). FEED-10 · LAY-08
  17. 17/listening drops the word “listening”. The freed column holds a 36px cover of the session’s newest release. The headline becomes “track — artist”, and “+ 15 more” replaces “· 16 songs +”. COL-09 · FEED-10
  18. 18An open session lists its tracks under the cover column, newest first, each with its own time. The day header keeps its useful “songs · min” and drops the artist count on phones. COL-09
  19. 19The empty plate. When art is missing or fails to load (onError), the cover becomes a hairline square with a plate mark, never the browser’s broken-image glyph. The same component serves top lists, session rows and album shelves. SYS-08
The tradeoff. Clamping reposts hides most of other people’s words: reading Poe’s whole dispatch takes a tap, and losing avatars removes the fastest way to recognise a regular. Typesetting every quote, including ones inside Dame’s own posts, means the ledger no longer matches the cards layout or record pages, so PostEmbed needs a ledger-only variant. The thread folio’s “1:46 am · from 1:27” is less natural than a plain range; it trades that for a column that never reverses. The horizon makes home much shorter, about three days instead of 554 rows. That is the point, but “Load the week before” needs real per-collection cursor paging: more requests, and a reader can now run out of feed. On desktop the bar’s “Oct 25” repeats the strip. On /logging the running dates replace the .day-section-header elements the strip reads its day label from, so that hook has to move.

Render the card as .ledger-ref (host in all-small-caps + title) and strip a title suffix equal to “— host”.

  • Horizon. With INITIAL_FETCH_MAX = 100 (Home.jsx:51), track for each collection that returned a cursor the createdAt of its oldest record. The horizon is the newest of those, floored to the start of the next whole day. Filter older rows and render a <LedgerHorizon> where the load sentinel sits (Home.jsx:768). “Load the week before” calls listRecords with each cursor. The ❧ fleuron isn’t in the Google Fonts subsets of Crimson Pro that index.html loads, so ship it as a small inline SVG.
  • Bottom bar. Swap the scrolledPast count (src/components/ChromeBar.jsx:919–927) for the short form of useCurrentDayLabel (:1111).
  • Single-type pages. Make FeedItem.jsx:300 pass showVerb into FeedLedgerRow; Posting.jsx:84 and Listening.jsx:152 already send false. Logging’s LEDGER_VERB_LABELS “dame.is” (FeedLedgerRow.jsx:59) becomes an inline small-caps prefix. On /logging the first row of a day takes the date cell and border-top: 1px solid var(--rule), and .feed-day-group + .feed-day-group (Feed.css:70) drops its --space-7. Give the date cell a data-day so useCurrentDayLabel (ChromeBar.jsx:1111), which queries .day-section-header .day-header, still finds the day. summarizeListen (:415) leads with the newest play’s “track — artist” and a cover.
  • Covers. Replace the local Cover in src/components/ListeningStats.jsx:188 with AlbumCover, whose onError already falls back to .album-cover-empty (src/components/AlbumCover.jsx:60–80). Restyle that class (src/pages/Albums.css:131) and .listen-rank-cover-empty (ListeningStats.css:191) as the plate: border: 1px solid var(--rule) on a --rule-soft mix, with an inset ::after hairline.

System

One set of controls: a button, an “on”, a figures band, two label voices and a sheet header, used everywhere

Today about eleven quiet buttons run from 27 to 40px tall. “Selected” is drawn five ways and numbers in six stat-block styles. Section heads come at 12, 14, 22 and 28px, and dates in five formats. The filter sheet shows all of it at once. Proposed: one small kit, set out like a type specimen and checked at 1 pm and 7 pm, and the filter sheet rebuilt from it as a book index.

7 pm

Phone, 1 pm and 7 pm. One column, rows of 44px or more on a coarse pointer, the gloss on a second line. “only” is its own target, set apart from the count, not fused to the toggle. At 7 pm (scrolled to the end) the header stays put, and the box and the type still separate on from off with no help from the tint.

  1. 1One Button, four tiers, three heights. Quiet, primary, text and icon share one base: 14px serif, sentence case, 0.02em, a square 1px hairline. They come at 28 (record actions, x-ray), 36 (default) and 44px (touch). Hover, focus and disabled are the same on every tier. Disabled is a dashed hairline instead of the grey 50% “Sign in to sign” slab. This replaces about 11 treatments at 27–40px, including four separately styled “load more” buttons. Small caps stay with labels, not actions. (SYS-01)
  2. 2One “on”. A 16% accent wash, an accent hairline and ink text. It is used for the filter box, the segmented “7 days”, open bar chips such as the filter chip while its sheet is open, and the layout toggle. That replaces today’s solid-accent tabs, black layout chip and dashed pills. Solid fill now only ever means “the primary action”. On/off is carried by a ☑/☐ box as well as colour. (SYS-02, INT-08, MOB-13)
  3. 3The open compass passes. Today it puts --page on --accent-soft: 2.0:1 at 1 pm and 2.8:1 at 7 pm, under the 3:1 a control needs. Open, it now takes the “on” look and shows ×: 13.0:1 and 5.9:1. At rest it stays filled with --accent-fill. c-06 keeps the fill when open instead. Either clears AA, but this way every open toggle in the bar looks the same. (SYS-02)
  4. 4One figures primitive, two layouts. A small-caps label sits above a 28px ink numeral in tabular figures, with an optional italic note under it. Cells align to the top, so “≈ 7.7 hrs” no longer lifts 463. “Ruled” is a hairline band with no outer box (listening, logging, exploring, Ratioed). “Inline” is the open colophon row (mothing’s 29 · 519 · 217, albums, a night, an album). Accent is kept for figures that are links. This replaces six stat-block styles and five copied stylesheets. (SYS-03, LAY-06, COL-07, IDN-11, TYP-06)
  5. 5One section head. 22px semibold, sentence case, with meta right-aligned on the same hairline. “36 SIGNATURES” becomes “Signatures … 36”, which is the home day head’s “Today … 23 items, 289 interactions” pattern. The same tier serves “Replies”, “Recent listening” and the résumé’s “Experience”. (SYS-05, TYP-09)
  6. 6Two label voices and a floor. The eyebrow is real capitals at 11px, weight 500 and 0.1em, in a muted ink that clears 4.5:1. Meta is 13px tabular. The scale is 48 · 28 · 22 · 16 · 14 · 13 · 11. That replaces 26 rendered sizes, 13 of them between 9.3 and 12.6px. Units keep their case (“65 dB”, not “65 DB”). (SYS-05, TYP-05)
  7. 7One date and time house style. Long dates read “January 29, 2025”, short “Jan 29, 2025”, clocks “3:17 pm”, and the hour chip “1 pm”. Relative times are used only under 30 days and are rounded the same way everywhere, so one post can’t read “1y ago” and “2 years ago” at once. ISO dates appear only in x-ray. Time columns use tabular figures. (SYS-11, TYP-10, TYP-06)
  8. 8One sheet header. A 44px row with an eyebrow title at the gutter, optional meta and text actions, and a 28px hairline × whose right edge sits over the compass. This header goes on BottomSheet, so info, filters, guestbook, time of day and open-in stop rebuilding it. “Time of day” keeps “Live” beside its ×. The filter title drops from 16px to 11px to match the others. (SYS-06)
  9. 9One reference card. PostEmbed’s link card and the Leaflet website block become one LinkCard, in a compact and a full size. Both get the same host eyebrow, title size, fill and --rule-soft hairline, which also replaces the undefined --text-md. The résumé’s “Selected work” stays an index list. (SYS-07)
  10. 10Proven at 7 pm. Every text pair in the strip clears 4.5:1 on the dusk tokens. Today’s black-mixed primary gives 3.3:1 at 7 pm, and --accent-fill (accent mixed 20% toward ink) gives 4.6:1. The “on” wash under ink gives 5.9:1. Labels use the muted ink that c-02 solves per hour; here it is drawn as --ink-muted mixed 30% toward --ink. (SYS-01, SYS-02)
  11. 11The filter sheet is an index. Lines are ruled, in two columns on desktop and one on a phone, under four group heads: words, making, noticing, social. Each reads ☑ gerund, gloss, dot leaders, then the count in tabular figures. Off lines get an empty box and muted type (5.3:1 or better on the sheet), not a white chip that outshines the “on” ones. Gerunds, counts and boxes line up on shared verticals. (FEED-08, LAY-12, INT-08, MOB-13)
  12. 12“only” stops shouting. On desktop it appears on the hovered or focused line, in a fixed column so nothing shifts. On a phone it is always shown, as its own target the full height of the row (44 × 57px), 12px clear of the count. Today’s 35 × 30px half-chip sits flush against the toggle. (FEED-08, MOB-13)
  13. 13Counts say what they are. Collections that hit the 100-record first fetch (Home.jsx:51) read “100+” instead of a total-looking “100”. “~85” stays the snapshot estimate, and flushing shows “—” because it isn’t loaded until switched on. The header reads “14 of 17 kinds · the defaults”, and the footer says what the numbers count. (INT-08, FEED-08)
The tradeoff. The cost is breadth, not difficulty. This touches about 60 button roots, five stat stylesheets, every small-caps label and every date call. Done piecemeal, the site would have two systems for a while, which is worse than one inconsistent one. It needs a short freeze and a stylelint rule, or it will drift again. The new eyebrow is visibly a little heavier than today’s synthesized small caps everywhere at once, so the chrome will look slightly less whispery. That is the point, but it is a change of voice and Dame should see it on a real page first. The filter index is taller than the chip cloud: about 490px on desktop against 265px. The glosses are new copy someone has to keep true as collections change. Making the open compass a wash rather than a fill (where c-06 keeps the fill) trades a little brand weight for one consistent “on”.

Signature features

X-ray keeps the page and writes its records in the margins, on every page

On a blog post x-ray reads like an annotated edition, but on home it swaps every row for an at:// line, hiding the posts it should explain, and it skips the live signals in the bar. Proposed: one marginalia grammar everywhere, where the content stays, the collection and the rkey/CID take the verb and time columns, every signal names its record (or admits it isn't one), and a tapped row opens its tree beside it.

Phones at 390px, on c-01's running head, and the grammar. Left, 1 pm: each row gains one caption line under its running head and keeps its content. Middle, 9 pm (content as at 1 pm): the tapped row's record opens directly under the caption you tapped, above the photo. Right: the three marks, measured.

  1. 1Every live signal names its source. Status, now-playing and the vitals get a dotted underline and a mono tag: is.dame.now; fm.teal.feed.play (the newest play — it reads fm.teal.actor.status while that hasn't expired); is.dame.state, one record behind all five vitals, so one underline spans them. Followers and the day count say in italic that they aren't records: an AppView count, and a sum from BIRTHDATE. Tapping any of them opens the same tree as a row. INT-03
  2. 2The hero phrases are records too. “an interface designer” and the opossum clause are is.dame.hero.phrase records (3mphmc3wnki2d, part: role; 3mpyjpejoxt2d, part: clause). Each gets the underline, with its tag at the end of its ruled line. “dame is” stays plain. INT-03
  3. 3The verb column becomes the collection. ‘posting’ becomes app.bsky.feed. / post, broken after the authority so it fits the existing 6.5rem column and nothing moves when x-ray toggles. Posts and reposts still tell apart at a glance. IDN-10, INT-03
  4. 4The content stays. Rows keep their height and their posts; text drops one step to --ink-muted (6.19:1 at 1 pm, 5.89:1 at 9 pm) instead of display: none or 35% opacity, which would fail AA. You can see which record is the dril image. IDN-10, INT-03
  5. 5The time column becomes the address. The rkey sits over a short CID; the rkey is a TID, so it still encodes the time. In x-ray the column widens to 5.5rem; the body's left edge doesn't move, and the body is capped at --measure anyway. IDN-10
  6. 6A bracket says “this is a record, and it opens”. A hairline bracket in the left margin marks each record row, the way blocks.text marks a paragraph, and the pointer becomes a hand over it. Today nothing says a row can be tapped. INT-03
  7. 7The HUD counts instead of shrugging. “71 records in this feed — tap a row to open its record” replaces “the protocol data”. DETAILS lists the page's collections with counts, linked to /exploring, instead of three dashes. INT-03
  8. 8A tapped row opens its tree in its own margin. Today's panel (pds → repo → collection → record → cid) moves into the empty right half of the row, beside the post, with the full at:// broken at each “/”. A repost also names its subject, Poe's post and its CID. Today the row prints that subject CID, bafyreid4…tja, beside the repost's own URI, whose CID is bafyreibz…iza. IDN-10, INT-03
  9. 9The HUD names what you're on. Hover, focus or tap puts that record's at:// in the bar, linked to its /exploring page, as the HUD already does on a blog post. IDN-10
  10. 10On phones, one caption line. Under c-01's running head, nsid/rkey and the short CID fit on one line (50 characters at 10.5px is about 315 of 358px). The caption is the row's accessible description, not aria-hidden. INT-03, IDN-10
  11. 11The panel opens under your thumb. On a phone the tree drops directly beneath the caption you tapped, above the photo. That keeps the “panel under the tap” behaviour that today's collapse was built to protect. INT-03
  12. 12One grammar, measured. Mono at 10.5–11px in one x-ray ink: dotted underlines for inline records, brackets for block records, italic serif for things that aren't records. The blog's blocks.text glosses join it. They are drawn at 62% opacity today, which gives 2.57:1 at 1 pm. IDN-10
The tradeoff. Rows no longer collapse, so x-ray home is as long as home. Scanning a day's addresses takes more scrolling than today's one-line manifest, and on a phone an open tree pushes the photo down. Two columns of mono, underlines in the bar and tags on the hero make the page busy. That's acceptable only because x-ray is opt-in, and it argues against ever making it a default. The tags need data the chrome doesn't keep today: NowStatus, NowPlaying, VitalsPanel and HeroSentence must hold the URI and CID of what they render. The x-ray ink is darker than the live accent by day. At 7 pm it reaches only 4.43:1 on --page, so that hour depends on c-02's contrast floor. And the “not a record” tags admit that two signals come from elsewhere, which some readers will take as a gap rather than candour.

Visitors

The guestbook becomes a visitors’ book you write in first and sign once

Today /welcoming reads like a comment thread: the count is the loudest type after the title, each note sits between a name stack and a CID line, and signing opens a sheet that wants a handle before you can write a word, behind a grey slab that looks broken. Proposed: a ruled register where the notes are the loudest thing, and a sign sheet that starts with the note, shows you the line you’ll leave, then signs with your handle in one hop.

Ready to sign at 7 pm (sky-19), and an empty book at 9 pm (sky-21). The note and handle are demo input (alice.bsky.social is the handle the audit typed into the live sheet). The empty book is the page column only, with no chrome; its copy keeps today’s line, which already speaks to the visitor.

  1. 1The intro leads with the note, on ruled paper. “Leave a note that you were here, and sign it with any atproto account” puts writing before signing in, as the sheet now does. The intro sits on the home hero’s 14% ink rules, so the page reads as a lined book from the first line. It is still the is.dame.page/guestbook record’s intro, so this is a content edit. INT-10.
  2. 2One section head. “Signatures” is 22 px semibold in sentence case. “36, newest first” is 13 px tabular meta on the same hairline, the home day head’s “Today … 23 items” pattern and c-11’s section tier. Today the count is a 28 px tracked-caps h2, the loudest type under the H1. TYP-09, COL-14.
  3. 3The next line is yours. The call to action becomes the book’s next blank line, numbered 37, with the page’s one filled button at its end. It opens the same sign sheet as today (and as the home page’s signature button), with the cursor in the note. The fill is the Resume primary on the shared --accent-fill (c-06, c-11), and --page on it is 6.50:1. INT-10.
  4. 4The note is the loudest thing. Each entry is a register line. Its number hangs in the margin, the note is 18 px ink (16.25:1), and beneath it runs a small-caps signature line: a 20 px square avatar, name, handle, then the place in the signer’s own words in italic, all in --ink-muted (6.19:1). A one-line entry takes about 90 px on desktop, against about 148 px today. COL-14.
  5. 5The date is the folio and the permalink. “Sep 1, 2026” closes the signature line on the right and links to the record page, as “1mo ago” does today. Dates are in Eastern time, like the sky. The CID fingerprint line leaves the default view. X-ray and the record page still show it. COL-14.
  6. 6The sheet opens on a header, not a paragraph. It uses c-11’s shared sheet header: the eyebrow “Sign the guestbook” and a 28 px hairline ×. The paragraph that restated the page intro is gone. INT-10.
  7. 7Write first. A serif textarea at 18 px on --page, “Leave a note…”, with a live “0 / 300” count (ENTRY_TEXT_MAX_GRAPHEMES; today it appears only under 40 left). “Signing from” folds behind “Add a place” until asked for. The note sits at the top of the full-height sheet, where the keyboard can’t cover it. INT-10.
  8. 8A proof of your line. The empty half of today’s sheet now shows the entry exactly as the register will set it: number 37, your note, your handle, “just now”. A fingerprint line says where it will live: on your own PDS, as an is.dame.guestbook.entry record. INT-10, COL-14.
  9. 9Then sign, once. The sheet has one handle field (handle, DID or PDS URL, as now) and one button, “Sign with atproto →”. Disabled is a dashed --rule hairline with --ink-muted text (5.67:1 on the sheet), not a 50% ink slab. One line says what happens: a hop to your PDS that asks for one permission, the existing repo:is.dame.guestbook.entry grant, then back here, signed. INT-10.
  10. 10Enabled is the site’s primary, at every hour. It is the same filled button as Resume, on --accent-fill. --page on it is 4.59:1 at 7 pm. Today’s black-mixed Resume fill gives 3.31:1 there, and today’s sign button is a near-black slab. INT-10.
  11. 11The preview is live, and the draft survives the hop. The proof updates as you type the note and the handle. Once the handle resolves, the public AppView can fill in your avatar and name. The button saves the draft to sessionStorage, and on return from OAuth the record is written from it. You land on /welcoming with your line on top: no second tap, no retyping. At 7 pm the muted ink on --page is drawn 30% toward --ink (4.88:1), the per-hour fix c-02 proposes. INT-10.
  12. 12An empty book that speaks to the visitor. This is the .empty-note primitive SYS-12 calls for, used here first. An NSID eyebrow sits over today’s own italic line, which already speaks to the visitor, and below them is the blank line numbered 1 with the primary. Nothing is indented, because .empty-note sets text-indent: 0 and the p + p prose rule can’t reach it. All text clears 5.89:1 at 9 pm. SYS-12, COL-11.
The tradeoff. Writing first moves the handle field low in the sheet, the spot today’s top-anchored field was placed to avoid. On iOS the keyboard will cover it, so focusing it has to scroll the sheet (a visualViewport inset or scroll-margin), and that needs testing on a real phone. Signing on return without a second tap makes the PDS consent screen the only confirmation. That is honest, since it names the one permission, but a signer who changes their mind there loses the draft once the tab closes. The margin numbers are derived from the public count, so hiding a signature renumbers every line above it. The flagged tally also only covers the first page, so later pages can be off until loaded. If that bothers you, drop the numbers: the register still works without them. Hiding the CID takes away a protocol detail some visitors liked, though x-ray keeps it one click away.

Every finding

All 130 verified findings, grouped by theme and ordered by severity. Each was checked by an independent verifier; where it corrected the detail or the severity, the corrected version is shown with its note. Evidence names refer to the capture corpus behind this audit.

1 The sky needs a floor: legible at every hour, paper by day, steady on arrival 13 findings · 5 high · 2 medium · 6 low

The palette is derived each hour with no contrast check. --ink-faint carries the ledger verbs and times, the day stats, the link-card hosts and the hero's 'dame is'. It measures 2.49:1 at 6am, 2.63:1 at 7pm and 2.50:1 at 8pm, clears 4.5:1 only at 7am and 9am, and at 7am it lands almost exactly on the accent. By day, the owner's surfaceSep tuning also scales --page-edge, so image mats, moth caption slabs and Exploring cards turn chrome-strength cyan. The tuning record arrives after first paint, so a cold load goes white → retired parchment → untuned cyan → tuned page, and the brand mark pops in and pushes the wordmark 34px right. After dark, white screenshots are the brightest objects on the page. The hour chip and its sheet don't distinguish frozen from live, have no hour labels, and use 10×20px cells on phones.

FEED-04highThe labels that structure the ledger (verb, time, day stats) are the smallest and lowest-contrast text on the page

accessibility · Home feed / activity ledger UX · effort M · verifier: confirmed · mockup c-02

/, /posting, /logging

What we saw. The verb and time columns, plus the day stats, are what make the ledger a ledger. They are all set in --ink-faint at 9.6–13.2px. In the sky palette that colour sits between 2.49:1 and 4.23:1 against the page for 22 of 24 hours. At dawn (h06) and dusk (h19–20) the labels nearly disappear (home__desktop__h06__s1.png). On mobile the rule `calc(var(--text-xs) * 0.8)` also drops the 1.1 --mono-scale, so Crimson Pro, which has a small x-height, renders at 9.6px.

Why it matters. Scanning a ledger means reading down the verb and time columns. When those columns can't be read, the page is just a stream of embeds, and low-vision readers lose the timeline entirely. The light and dark themes had --ink-faint re-tuned, but the sky palette, the only theme actually shipped, did not.

Recommendation. Use --ink-muted for the verb and time text (6.19:1 at h13 and 3.98:1 at h19, still to be tuned), and keep --ink-faint for rules only. Alternatively, add a floor to skyTheme.js so --sky-ink-faint reaches at least 4.5:1 against --sky-page every hour. Keep labels at least 12px on mobile: drop the 0.8× step once FEED-01 stacks the labels and frees the width. Small caps with 0.06em tracking can carry the 'marginal note' look instead of pale colour.

Verifier. I re-ran skycontrast.mjs on the is.dame.sky tuning record. --sky-ink-faint on --sky-page reaches 4.5:1 only at h07 (5.50) and h09 (4.97). It is 2.49 at h06, 2.63 at h19, 2.50 at h20, 3.79 at h13 and at most 4.23 elsewhere, so 22 of 24 hours fail. The metrics JSON shows the same 2.49:1 on 'posting' (ledger-verb) and '3:17 PM' (ledger-time) at h06. The labels are barely visible in home__desktop__h06__s1.png, home__desktop__h19__s1.png and home__mobile__h19__s0.png. Sizes check out: 13.2px and 11.22px on desktop, 9.6px on mobile (Feed.css:2419-2423 drops --mono-scale). --ink-muted is 6.19 at h13 and 3.98 at h19, as stated. The more precise prior reference is RECOMMENDATIONS §3.3 (sky derivation has no contrast floor) together with §3.1. Both are still open for the sky palette.
